explanation: Israeli traffic regulations set maximum permitted dimensions for each vehicle category, and the legal maximum overall length for a bus is capped at 15 meters, regardless of body style.

Blue tourist-information pictograms mark services for travelers, and this specific icon (depicting bunk-style beds) is the standard symbol reserved for a youth hostel, distinct from hotel or campsite icons.
This tourist-service pictogram uses a tent/vehicle icon to mark an official site set aside for camping or overnight parking, distinguishing it from a simple rest stop or memorial marker.
A plain red circular sign with no vehicle-type exception shown is the strongest prohibition sign, meaning the road is completely closed to all vehicles approaching from either direction.
Route-number signs are color-coded by road classification; the blue rectangular shield format used here identifies the number of a limited-access freeway (motorway), not a local or regional road.

Following the standard sign-design convention used throughout the warning-sign category, hazard signs are triangular with the apex pointing up, so drivers can recognize a warning by shape alone even before reading it.

This overhead advance sign is posted before a junction specifically to show which movement (straight, left, right) is permitted from each lane, letting drivers position themselves correctly before reaching the intersection.

In the standard signal sequence, showing red and yellow together is a transition phase that warns a stopped driver the light is about to turn green, so they can prepare to move off without yet entering the junction.

Curbstone color-coding supplements posted signs; a red-yellow marking denotes a strict zone where even brief stopping is forbidden, with the only exception being vehicle types specifically authorized by an accompanying sign.
This is the cancellation version of a no-overtaking sign, marked to show that the overtaking ban imposed earlier along the road no longer applies beyond this point.
Water on the road sharply reduces tire grip, and because skid and rollover risk grow with the square of speed, a wet surface makes higher speeds disproportionately more dangerous for control loss.

The law requires any vehicle used to transport children to hold specific approval from the Ministry of Transport for that purpose; an ordinary bus or car is not automatically qualified just because children are aboard.
Student buses are designed so boarding happens only through the front right door facing the curb, keeping children away from moving traffic on the road side of the vehicle.

"Pupil transport" has a specific legal definition: it is transport of children to school or an organized activity carried out in a vehicle that has been formally authorized for that purpose, not any bus ride involving children.
Because standing children lack seatbelts or secure handholds, safety rules require every child on a school bus to be seated, making it prohibited to carry children standing while the bus is moving.
Tunnels reduce natural light and visibility even during the day, so the rule for a tunnel marked with this sign requires drivers to switch on their front (regular) lights so they can see and be seen.
A blue circular sign with a bicycle pictogram is a mandatory-instruction sign designating the marked path for the exclusive use of bicycles, not shared with pedestrians or motor vehicles.
Unless a supplementary plate or another sign states otherwise, the effect of this type of regulatory sign ends automatically once the next intersection is reached.
A "tour vehicle" is legally classified as a bus-type vehicle carrying passengers, so its driver must hold a class D or D1 license, the categories required for driving buses of that size.

Because a tour vehicle combines passenger transport with guiding duties, the law requires its driver to be both a certified tour guide approved by the Ministry of Tourism and a holder of a class D or D1 driving license.
The wheelchair-symbol parking sign reserves that space specifically for vehicles displaying the official disability permit referenced on the sign, not for handicapped-accessible vehicles in general.
This sign's lane diagram shows an added lane joining the roadway, warning drivers in advance that the number of travel lanes on the road is about to increase.
This sign's lane diagram shows lanes merging together, warning drivers in advance that the number of travel lanes on the road is about to decrease and they may need to merge.
This tourist-service pictogram uses a fork-and-knife style icon, the standard symbol identifying a restaurant rather than a hotel or refreshment stand.
This tourist-service pictogram (a cup-style icon) is the standard symbol used to mark a bar or coffee shop, distinct from icons for lodging or washrooms.
Gravity accelerates a vehicle on a long or steep downhill grade and strains the brakes, so a driver must slow down and use a lower gear to keep the vehicle under control on the descent.

Sidewalk parking is only an exception to the normal rule, and this sign permits it solely according to the sidewalk's own markings, and only for private and commercial vehicles up to 2,200 kg gross weight.
This sign marks a residential street set aside where children are expected to play, requiring drivers to treat the whole roadway as a pedestrian-priority area and drive with extra caution.
This sign marks the start of a designated speed-limited zone, where the maximum permitted speed for the marked area is set at 30 km/h to protect pedestrians, children, and cyclists on that street.
This is the cancellation sign for a play-street zone, marked with a diagonal strike to show that the play-street restrictions in force earlier along the road no longer apply beyond this point.

This sign marks the entrance to a zone where a combination of special traffic restrictions applies throughout the marked area, rather than stating one single numeric limit, until a matching end-of-zone sign is reached.
This is the cancellation sign posted where a 30 km/h speed-limited zone ends; from this point the general speed limit for that type of road resumes until another sign states otherwise.
Road markings are color-coded by function, and a yellow line pattern like this one is used specifically to mark a lane reserved for public transport rather than an ordinary travel lane.

A broken white line is the standard marking used simply to separate lanes traveling in the same direction, indicating the road's direction of travel and lane boundaries rather than forbidding crossing.

A ladder-style pattern painted across the full width of the road, similar to a pedestrian zebra crossing but intended for cyclists, marks a designated crossing point where cyclists have priority to cross.
A continuous separation line marks a boundary that must not be crossed, so a driver on this side of it is prohibited from driving to the left of the line into the opposing or restricted lane.
When a vehicle is shown positioned on the right side of a continuous separation line, the rule is to keep driving on that right side and never cross the solid line under any circumstance.
A blue sign combining a bicycle symbol with a directional arrow designates a mandatory one-directional path reserved exclusively for bicycle traffic.

This transitional marking (broken line thickening toward solid) is a warning that a continuous separation line is about to begin, alerting the driver that crossing or overtaking will soon no longer be allowed.
When a broken line runs alongside a continuous line, only the driver on the side where the broken line appears may cross to overtake, while the driver facing the solid line side may not.
The vehicle shown is positioned on the side of the continuous line, so it must keep driving to the right of the lines and is barred from crossing the solid separation line to overtake or pass.
Crossing a combined line marking is only allowed from the side where the broken line lies next to the continuous line, which is the situation shown on the left in this scenario.
This marking is used along road edges lacking a physical curbstone, tracing the boundary of the paved roadway so drivers can judge the road's edge, especially in poor visibility.
An arrow painted in the left lane pointing left indicates that, at the approaching junction, that lane is reserved solely for left turns rather than continuing straight.
A combined straight-and-left arrow painted in a lane indicates both movements are authorized from that lane, so a driver in it may continue straight ahead or turn left.
Because only the left lane carries a left-turn arrow, the marking restricts left turns to that lane in the driver's own direction of travel, not to every lane approaching the junction.
A solid line marked across a lane at a junction functions as a stop line: the designated point where a vehicle must stop whenever a rule (a sign, signal, or crossing) requires stopping there.
A stop line only compels a driver to halt when another rule, such as a stop sign, red light, or level crossing, makes stopping mandatory at that spot, not as a stand-alone command to always stop.
A zebra pattern of parallel white stripes painted across the road marks a pedestrian crossing, where by law drivers must give right of way to pedestrians using it.
Signs in this reference series are numbered consecutively, so the sign that comes immediately after number 708 in the sequence is number 709.
An arrow painted inside a driving lane pointing left shows that vehicles in that lane are required to turn left at the upcoming intersection, rather than continue straight.
A yellow arrow marking is reserved specifically for public transport vehicles, granting buses an exclusive straight-ahead movement at the intersection that private vehicles are not authorized to use.

The law restricts a new driver, defined as someone with under two years of licensed driving or under 21 years old, from carrying more than two passengers in a private car unless a qualified escort sits beside them, reducing the peer-pressure distraction linked to young-driver accidents.
Braking distance is defined narrowly as the distance covered from the moment the brakes are actually applied until the vehicle comes to a complete stop, excluding the driver's earlier reaction time.

Regulations tie the rear fog lamp's operation to the front lights being switched on, preventing its very bright beam from being used unnecessarily while ensuring the vehicle's front lighting is also active.
White-painted areas of various shapes on the roadway mark constructed or painted traffic islands that separate different traffic flows and must not be driven over.
Alternating blue curbstones denote a parking area regulated by the local authority's own conditions, which typically require payment, unlike unrestricted or disability-only parking zones.
Alternating red-white curbstones mark a stretch where stopping is prohibited for ordinary vehicles, with the sole exception of public transport vehicles loading or unloading passengers.
This road marking designates an area where parking is prohibited entirely, typically used to keep sightlines or access clear near junctions or building entrances.
Since total stopping distance equals reaction distance plus braking distance, and reaction distance is always greater than zero, the stopping distance must always exceed the braking distance alone.
This marking designates a stopping place for the specific vehicle types indicated by an accompanying sign, used at locations where no physical lay-by or pull-off area is available.
Where a lay-by and curbstones are present, this marking permits stopping only for the vehicle types specified by the signpost placed at that location, not for vehicles generally.
Painted bay or box markings define individual vehicle parking spaces, and the rule is that parking is allowed only inside a marked space, not anywhere else along that stretch.
Under standard traffic-signal rules, a red light is an absolute instruction to stop the vehicle and remain stationary at the line until the signal changes.
This reinforces the core signal rule that a driver facing red must not continue driving at all for as long as the red light remains lit.

A green signal grants permission to proceed but does not itself guarantee the intersection is safe or clear, so the driver may keep driving only after confirming the intersection is actually clear and safe to enter.
A steady (non-flashing) yellow light means the signal is about to turn red, so the driver must stop before the intersection unless already so close that stopping safely is no longer possible.

A flashing yellow light signals that the signal is operating in a caution mode rather than controlling right of way directly, so drivers must proceed carefully following whatever signs are posted at that intersection.
A green directional arrow only authorizes movement in the exact direction it points, so a driver may proceed solely in that direction and not straight ahead or any other way.
This sign's converging-arrow pictogram indicates the lane ahead is ending, so traffic from either side must merge together into the remaining lane.

Worn tread has less depth to channel water away and grip the road surface, so the more worn-out a tire is, the greater the risk of skidding on a wet road, which is why a minimum legal tread depth is required.
This flashing signal near a crossing point is a caution warning, meaning the driver may continue but must proceed carefully and give way to any pedestrians crossing the road at that point.

This is a dedicated level-crossing signal, and while it is flashing it functions as a mandatory stop instruction that remains in force for the entire duration of the flashing, since a train may be approaching.
A flashing red signal at a level crossing requires the driver to stop and stay stopped as long as the light keeps flashing, since it warns that a train is approaching or passing.
A lane-control signal displaying a permissive indication above a lane means that lane is currently open, so driving in it is permitted.
As with other lane-control gantry signals, a permissive indication shown above this lane means the lane is currently open and driving in it is permitted.
A lane-control signal displaying a prohibitive indication (such as a cross) above a lane closes that lane to traffic, so driving in it is not permitted and vehicles must merge elsewhere.
When this signal is lit above a driving lane, it closes that specific lane to traffic, meaning driving in it is prohibited until the indication changes.
This overhead sign closes the lane beneath it to traffic, instructing drivers not to enter or continue driving in that lane and to merge out in time.
This sign's pictogram depicts crossing gates, warning drivers in advance that the level crossing ahead is equipped with a physical barrier mechanism.
A lowered, horizontal crossing barrier is a physical and legal command that a train is imminent or passing, so every vehicle must stop before it and not attempt to continue past.

Like other curb and edge color-coding, this black-white marking is used purely to make sidewalks and traffic islands next to the road more visible, and carries no stopping or parking restriction of its own.
This sign warns of a point where the road narrows or an obstacle sits within the roadway, prompting drivers to slow down and take care passing that section.
This chevron sign requires a driver to slow down and follow only the direction physically shown by the arrows on the sign, rather than choosing their own path through the junction.
This warning sign's T-shaped diagram, with the side road joining from the left, warns drivers in advance of an approaching T-junction on their left.
This standard warning sign, showing a worker with a shovel, alerts drivers to construction or maintenance activity ahead, requiring reduced speed and extra caution.
Because the footbrake alone does not guarantee a parked vehicle stays in place, the parking (hand) brake must always be applied whenever the vehicle is left parked, regardless of the terrain.
For balanced handling and braking, the two wheels sharing an axle must be the same size and match the manufacturer's specifications, since mismatched tires cause uneven grip and instability.
The parking (hand) brake's core purpose is to hold a stationary vehicle in place through its own mechanical system, independent of the footbrake, so the vehicle doesn't move while parked.
These reflective roadside posts mark the road's edge and alignment, helping drivers follow the road's course, especially useful at night or through curves.
Orange coloring on signs or road markings is the standard convention specifically used to denote a road-works zone, distinguishing temporary work-site signage from permanent white or yellow signs.
Because the hand (parking) brake operates through a mechanism independent of the footbrake's hydraulic system, it is the correct immediate response for slowing the vehicle if the foot brake fails.

The rule is to stop before the stop line, but if a marked pedestrian crossing lies between the stop line and the intersection, the driver must stop even earlier, before that crossing, to keep it clear for pedestrians.
This weight-restriction sign specifies an exact threshold, in this case vehicles over 10,000 kg, above which commercial vehicles are barred from parking in the road section that follows the sign.
A restriction sign of this type remains in effect continuously along the road, regardless of distance or intervening junctions, until a specific sign cancelling it is posted.

Seat belts, head restraints, and airbags are passive-safety features that work together to reduce injury severity once a collision is already happening, by restraining occupants, preventing whiplash, and cushioning impact.

Right-of-way at a junction is set by the signs, signals, or approach directions shown in the scene, and here only the blue vehicle has priority over your path, so it alone must be given the right of way while you retain priority over the rest.

At an intersection without traffic signs, a road user approaching from your right holds right of way, and this default rule applies to cyclists exactly as it does to motor vehicles, so the cyclist coming from that side must be given priority.

Absent traffic signs, right-of-way is decided by each road user's direction of approach relative to yours, and in this scene both the motorcyclist and the cyclist are approaching from directions that place them ahead of you, so both must be allowed to go first.

When no signs regulate a junction and vehicles arrive together, the default is to give way to traffic approaching from your right and take priority over traffic on your left, setting the order shown: the vehicle on your right enters first, you follow, and the vehicle on your left goes last.
